facts.statement: Philadelphia writer, 1771–1810; trained for law before writing and editing.
Published Wieland (1798), Ormond (1799), Arthur Mervyn (1799–1800) and Edgar Huntly (1799).

interpretation.note: Interpretation of the documented life and works; no claim of personal acquaintance from shared themes.

appraisal.note: AETERNUS editorial judgement; not presented as a historical quotation.

en.tagline: The American republic discovers its Gothic shadows.
en.intro: Brown brought the Gothic novel into the houses, cities and unsettled spaces of the young United States. Fear arises from the failure to know another person, to trust a voice or to reconstruct an event.
en.orientation: His fiction takes American settings seriously as places of intellectual and moral uncertainty. The disturbance comes from within the new society.
origin: Born in Philadelphia, Brown first prepared for law. Writing and magazine editing became his principal occupation.
career: An extraordinary concentration of novels at the end of the 1790s established his place in early American fiction. Editorial and political writing continued alongside the works now most often remembered.
literature: Wieland and Edgar Huntly build their plots around uncertain knowledge. Explanations arrive through witnesses who may themselves misunderstand what they report.
en.legacy: Brown made the instability of perception a subject for American fiction. His novels ask readers to weigh a narrative while being drawn into it.
en.bridge: The editions recover the unease and intellectual pressure of the early American Gothic.
